pages.text: After lunch break at school, banana peels, orange peels, and yam peels lay scattered near the edge of the yard. “We can care for our compound better than this,” said Jamila. Awuku nodded. “Let us ask our teacher.”
sentences: After lunch break at school, banana peels, orange peels, and yam peels lay scattered near the edge of the yard.
“We can care for our compound better than this,” said Jamila.
Awuku nodded.
“Let us ask our teacher.”
pages.alt: In a Ghanaian schoolyard after lunch, Awuku and Jamila look thoughtfully at scattered banana and orange peels near a tree.

pages.text: Their teacher showed them how to build a compost heap. In a quiet corner of the school garden, they dug a shallow pit and layered fruit peels, dry brown leaves, and a sprinkle of garden soil. They kept plastic, bones, and glass completely out.
sentences: Their teacher showed them how to build a compost heap.
In a quiet corner of the school garden, they dug a shallow pit and layered fruit peels, dry brown leaves, and a sprinkle of garden soil.
They kept plastic, bones, and glass completely out.
pages.alt: Under their teacher’s guidance in the school garden, Jamila tips fruit peels from a bowl into a shallow earth pit while Awuku adds dry brown leaves.

pages.text: Each week, Awuku turned the heap gently with a long wooden stick. “Whew, it smells a little!” he laughed. “It smells like damp earth,” smiled Jamila, “and that is a good sign.” Afterwards, they blanketed the heap with dry leaves to keep flies away.
sentences: Each week, Awuku turned the heap gently with a long wooden stick.
“Whew, it smells a little!” he laughed.
“It smells like damp earth,” smiled Jamila, “and that is a good sign.” Afterwards, they blanketed the heap with dry leaves to keep flies away.
pages.alt: Awuku turning the garden compost heap with a wooden stick while Jamila spreads a tidy layer of dry leaves over the top.

pages.text: After several weeks, the peels had turned into dark, crumbly compost. “Tiny helpers in the soil—earthworms and microscopic living things—break plant waste down,” explained their teacher. “They turn old peels into rich food for the soil.”
sentences: After several weeks, the peels had turned into dark, crumbly compost.
“Tiny helpers in the soil—earthworms and microscopic living things—break plant waste down,” explained their teacher.
“They turn old peels into rich food for the soil.”
pages.alt: Close view of rich, dark, crumbly garden compost in the pit with a healthy earthworm wriggling through the damp soil.

pages.text: Awuku and Jamila mixed the finished compost into the vegetable beds. Soon the garden greens grew taller and brighter than ever. “Our lunch peels came back as food for the plants!” said Jamila proudly. “Nothing went to waste.”
sentences: Awuku and Jamila mixed the finished compost into the vegetable beds.
Soon the garden greens grew taller and brighter than ever.
“Our lunch peels came back as food for the plants!” said Jamila proudly.
“Nothing went to waste.”
pages.alt: Awuku and Jamila spreading dark compost around thriving, lush green leafy vegetables in the sunny school garden.

pages.text: Meanwhile, old plastic wrappers collected by the fence had not rotted at all. “Plastic does not break down like plant peels,” said their teacher. “So plastic goes into the waste bin, and peels go into the compost.” Afterwards, everyone washed their hands with soap and clean water.

pages.alt: Beside two colour-coded unlabelled school bins—one holding plastic wrappers and one holding fruit peels—Awuku and Jamila wash their hands with soap at a Veronica bucket tap.

activities.question: What breaks plant peels down into rich compost?
options: Earthworms and tiny living things in the soil

activities.question: Where should plastic wrappers be placed?

activities.prompt: Put the school composting steps in order.
items: Layer peels, dry leaves, and a little soil.
Turn the heap weekly and cover it with dry leaves.
Mix the dark crumbly compost into garden beds.

activities.definition: Decayed plant matter that enriches soil and helps plants grow.

glossary.definition: Rotted plant waste that makes rich, dark food for garden soil.
The outer skins removed from fruits and vegetables.
Soft and breaking easily into small, soil-like pieces.
